locator.quote: “If you were doing a movie, you can do close shots and frame the audience’s attention that way. But in theater we have to do a lot of it with lighting and sound. So we rely a lot on the lighting designer to train the eye of the audience. But we also, in terms of sound, want to keep everything moving along and keep it cohesive.”

claim: Lighting and sound designers in theatre collaboratively use lighting, sound volumes, and placement to guide audience attention and create cohesive storytelling experiences in real time, which differs fundamentally from film where camera framing can direct focus.
source_title: How Walter Trarbach Bridges the Gap Between Broadway's Golden Age and Schmigadoon!

locator.quote: “It’s such a crazy thing. I think it’s a wild job because sound design barely even exists. It only happens when the show is happening, right? And for most of the show, we’re not making sound. We’re just taking the sound that everybody else makes, all the performers, and then we basically just set the relative volumes of it and send it out to the speakers to the audience at relative volume levels depending where they’re sitting and what they need.”

locator.quote: “It’s almost like curating exactly what the audience should be hearing out of everything that’s done on stage,” explained Trarbach. “We put microphones on every actor, every musician. I think there may be like 18 or 20 microphones in the percussion area alone because they’ve got all these little things. Then we just kind of take it moment by moment and we try to mix the songs, try and make them sound a little better every time we do it.”

locator.quote: AC: All the theaters are so unique. And it depends on what type of theater it is. When I say that, I mean, is it a grid theater that has a fixed grid above, or is it a fly house that has a fly rail where you could bring scenery in and out from above? Is it in the round? Is it alley? Most designers would say they design for the space. You’re designing for the play, of course, but you also design for the space. What I mean by that is the size of the theater. An Importance of Being Earnest on an 80 foot wide theater is going to look very different from an Importance of Being Earnest that’s in a 20 foot wide thrust theater. You also want to fit the space, the set wants to fit nicely in the space as well. And with all that being said, the goal for us is always to focus on the actors. So a lot of the time in these bigger theaters, our goal is to focus in, to really keep our eye where the action is, which is the actors in the play.

claim: Professional scenic designers approach their work by deeply understanding the narrative, the spatial constraints of the theatre, and by collaborating closely with directors and technical teams, often iterating through rehearsals to refine designs to fit both story and venue.
source_title: Andrew Cohen: A Behind the Scenes on Set Design

locator.quote: This was very much a how do we establish we’re in the graveyard with your Spanish oak tree versus how we show that we’re inside the house now, at their dining table. How do we get from this scene to that scene, a lot of that kind of logistical thing. The design is traditional wing and drop, which means there’s portals and it staggers back in space. They still use it on Broadway today and it’s a great way, especially in this theater, which is a great theater, to tie this all together. It doesn’t have a fly system, so it’s not easy to get big scenery. You can’t get big scenery from above because there is no above, but there’s a fixed grid. So we have a lot of tracking things that come on and off. Affixed to our grid, to get things that get on stage quickly and safely and change up the scene a lot. So there’s a lot of things in the set that are tracks that help bring the space alive and surprise us a bit.

locator.quote: The Bard's tragedy gets blasted into orbit, transformed into a cosmic Glam rock comedy featuring norse gods, gladiator pits, space misfits and a golden robot.Containing adult language, puppet violence and at least one song that Shakespeare definitely didn't write, it is the ultimate treat for fans of Operation Mincemeat, Avenue Q and Forbidden Planet.Lewis Aves.It's Shakespeare. In space. With Norse hammers. And Muppet-like aliens running amok.We caught up with Dan Sturman, composer, lyricist, book writer, scenic designer, sound designer, graphic designer, puppet maker, scenic builder and set designer, to learn more.Hamlet is perhaps the most famous tragedy in the English language. At what exact moment did you say to yourself, "This needs space Vikings, violent puppets, and a David Bowie-inspired glam rock soundtrack"?It hit us when we realized that the high-stakes melodrama and cosmic angst of Shakespeare’s original play actually mirror the theatricality of 1970s glam rock. Hamlet’s existential dread feels right at home on a galactic stage surrounded by space Vikings and chaotic, Muppet-style alien puppets. Combining classic tragedy with sci-fi absurdity felt like the ultimate way to bring fresh energy and big laughs to a centuries-old story.The show draws comparisons to irreverent hits like Operation Mincemeat, Avenue Q, and Forbidden Planet. How do you balance genuine Shakespearean drama with madcap sci-fi comedy without losing the core emotional stakes of Prince Hamlet’s journey?We keep the structural backbone of Shakespeare’s narrative intact—at its heart, it is still a straight, punchy adaptation of Prince Hamlet seeking revenge for his father. The humor comes from the outrageous environment, high-energy score and eccentric characters surrounding him. By treating Hamlet’s emotional journey with sincerity amid the cosmic chaos, the comedy hits harder without undercutting the tragic stakes.How did you go about world-building the Denmark System and its lore? Did setting it in a distant galaxy unlock new narrative solutions that Shakespeare’s original setting couldn't offer?Reframing the kingdom as the "Denmark System" allowed us to push every element to its absolute maximum. Deep Space also gave us the freedom to explore what happens to Hamlet after he is temporarily banished from his “home planet” with gladiatorial pits, alien creatures and high-tech weaponry, giving classic conflicts a fresh visual language. We play with familiar tropes, after all, when you strip away the period costumes, is Prince Hamlet’s classic journey really all that different from Luke Skywalker’s?David Bowie’s influence looms large over sci-fi and rock theatre. How does the glam rock sound mirror Hamlet’s internal existential crisis and theatrical angst?Glam rock is a broad church and in it you have everything from the classic rock and roll right up to Art-rock that defines 70s Bowie and his peers so well. So there is room for angst, fear, reflection, ambition and wonder all inside our musical world. We’re not just Bowie of course, he’s just the king of this genre. In addition to a glam rock sound, we also have more cinematic space music, Ska, ballad, comedy songs, but it all is held together in its own strange eclectic way that feels true to the genre.The show notes mention "at least one song that Shakespeare definitely didn't write." Without giving away too much, what can you tell us about the most outlandish or unexpected musical number in the score?Without spoiling the surprise, one standout crowd favourite is "The Game". It’s a powerful, show-stopping duet where two of our female leads take a sharp, modern look at how women are routinely ignored and sidelined by the warring men around them. It brings incredible musical fire while putting a fresh, unexpected spotlight on the story. Our diverts from Shakespeare in that Ophelia is involved in the storyline until the end, rather just wondering off to kill herself.Nic Gordon.You're based in the UK and your co-writer R.C. Staab is based in New York. After working together for over a dozen years, what does your songwriting process look like across the Atlantic? How do you pass ideas back and forth? We’ve been collaborating across the Atlantic for over 16 years, so distance is second nature to us now. We pass lyric drafts, audio memos, and scene ideas back and forth across time zones constantly. The delay actually helps us reflect on ideas before bouncing them back. Fortunately, today it’s so much easier to connect with Google Docs and talking and texting via WhatsApp.From Zombie Wedding at the NYC Fringe Festival to Space Hamlet in London, how has your collaborative dynamic evolved over the past decade? We’ve developed a shorthand where we trust each other’s instincts implicitly. Over the years, we've gotten bolder with our concepts—taking wild, high-concept ideas like zombie nuptials or space Vikings and structuring them into tight, full-throttle musical comedies. We’ve both gone and worked on different shows either solo or with other collaborators, but I think we enjoy working together more than anything.Puppets often carry a reputation for being strictly for children—unless you're Avenue Q or The Muppets doing a late-night set. What role do the puppets play in Space Hamlet, and how do you write music that fits puppet choreography? The idea of the using Muppet-style alien puppets came very late into the project, long after the script was finished and the songs. The director suggested Muppets as a Greek chorus and for a few key one-off character roles. We’ve grown quite fond of our furry friends. They add an element of pure visual fun that contrasts brilliantly with the dramatic storyline.The show enjoyed a sold-out run with Open Door Theatre in Norwich in 2025 before making the leap to London. What did you learn from the Norwich audiences, and how has the show changed or tightened for its London premiere?The Norwich run showed us how well the humor and music connected across all age groups. Moving to The Cockpit in London—a venue with superior technical and staging capabilities—allowed us to upgrade the entire production. We’ve tightened the emotional beats, added richer choreography, enhanced the LED set design and elevated the sound design to deliver an even bigger experience.How do you hope traditional Shakespeare aficionados react to Space Hamlet? Have any hardcore Bard fans surprised you with their feedback? We hope Bard enthusiasts appreciate that, under all the glam rock and space-viking flair, we maintain a genuine respect for the original play’s narrative drive. Classic fans are often the ones who enjoy it most because they spot all the subtle adaptations, line references, and clever twists we’ve baked into the sci-fi setting. An artistic director at the Norwich Theatre Royal said it best: “Space Hamlet was an amazing way of sharing the story of Hamlet to an audience that might otherwise not have been introduced to Shakespeare.”If you could ask Shakespeare a question about Hamlet, what would you choose to ask him?We'd ask him: "How do you feel about electric guitars, LED-lit space rocks and a golden robot playing your lead roles?" We like to think he was enough of a showman to appreciate the spectacle.What was the first piece of theatre that had a big impact on you?It probably was The Phantom Of The Opera. Somehow I had seen The Rocky Horror Picture Show way too young but that’s a movie, and it cemented a love for musicals but also for stories set in strange worlds to explore. Phantom has great music and design, but I think the storytelling is so focused it's like a laser that builds right up to that perfect final 15-minute scene. If our Hamlet aspires to anything, it's to have our score and our storytelling be something that builds up to the final duel scene where all the passions and energy at at explosive levels.What would you hope someone takes away from seeing Space Hamlet?We want audiences to leave energized, humming the songs and thoroughly entertained. Whether you know every line of Shakespeare or haven't read a word of it, we hope you walk away having experienced a fun, unique night of glam rock musical theatre while appreciating Shakespeare’s most intriguing work.Space Hamlet runs at The Cockpit Theatre in London from 22nd until 31st October 2026. For tickets visit https://www.thecockpit.org.uk/show/space_hamletYou can find out more about the show by visiting https://www.spacehamletmusical.com/

locator.quote: At the heart of AuraLuxMuse are two key modules: Lighting-Aligned Music Pretraining (LAMP), which performs contrastive learning between audio and lighting cues for alignment, and Preference-Adaptive Mixture of Experts (PAMoE), which conditions preference-aware cue retrieval and adaptation on designers’ intent through a gated ensemble of style-specific expert networks. To support training and evaluation, we introduce Musilux, the first dataset of paired musical audio and professional lighting cue sequences under diverse performance scenarios. We evaluate AuraLuxMuse across both virtual simulation environments and professional-grade laboratories. Experimental results, including objective and subjective evaluation, demonstrate that AuraLuxMuse retrieves and adapts stage-lighting cues that are visually cohesive, semantically meaningful, and artistically expressive, showing its potential for AI-assisted aesthetic stage design.

claim: AI-assisted stage lighting design systems like AuraLuxMuse use advanced deep-learning techniques to align musical audio with lighting cues, showing potential for stylistic adaptation and retrieval of lighting designs to support designers, but they face challenges with standardized parameters and comprehensive evaluation.
source_title: AuraLuxMuse: Adaptive Fusion Modeling for Aesthetic Stage Lighting Design with Music and Expert Guidance

locator.quote: Consequently, there is a compelling need for a system capable of modeling and automating the entire stage lighting design process. However, existing machine-learning systems typically restrict lighting control to basic properties such as light position and intensity, overlooking critical expressive dimensions including color, stylistic variation, and temporal rhythm. To the best of our knowledge, this topic has not been systematically explored under modern deep-learning paradigms. With advances in deep audio representation learning, it is now feasible to encode the latent structure of music in high-dimensional embedding spaces, providing a promising foundation for music-driven lighting synthesis. Three key challenges remain. The first is lack of structured parameterization: there is no standardized formulation for decomposing lighting attributes into learnable parameters. The second is multimodal alignment and personalization: learning effective correspondences between music and lighting remains difficult, particularly when integrating personalized and stylistic preferences. The third is the absence of comprehensive evaluation metrics: existing benchmarks fail to assess lighting quality in terms of both objective fidelity and subjective perception.

claim: AI-assisted stage lighting design systems like AuraLuxMuse use advanced deep-learning techniques to align musical audio with lighting cues, showing potential for stylistic adaptation and retrieval of lighting designs to support designers, but they face challenges with standardized parameters and comprehensive evaluation.
source_title: AuraLuxMuse: Adaptive Fusion Modeling for Aesthetic Stage Lighting Design with Music and Expert Guidance

locator.quote: Training excludes the validation and test assets and contains approximately 150 minutes of paired music and lighting cues. Validation covers six styles with two held-out examples per scenario and supplies manual references for the main-paper comparison. Test uses six unseen tracks across the six styles on a stage excluded from training. This is a controlled, style-balanced check of unseen music and unseen stage layout, not a population-scale benchmark; full-length expert/non-expert scoring limits its practical sample size. A cue-statistic t-SNE analysis over 14 stage-level output vectors yields a mean pairwise z-scored distance of 5.409±1.7465.409\pm 1.746, indicating multiple statistic regimes rather than collapse to a single template. The real-world demo stage is unseen; its nearest cue-statistic neighbors are the dance and rock stage cases. Because the t-SNE uses available cue-output vectors rather than the complete raw Musilux corpus, we treat it as supplementary descriptive evidence, not as a standalone generalization metric.

locator.quote: But the image that actually seeded the piece, Crowner says, was not a historical one. It was her own daily walk into her Red Hook studio, through a courtyard sometimes overrun with weeds and willow trees, and into a room flooded with skylight. “I always kind of have the feeling of nature, whether it’s through light or through certain botanical forms,” she says. “In my head, as you start to work.” She had been making a series of large green paintings around the time she and Tanowitz began talking. When Tanowitz visited the studio, they began to wonder: what if those paintings could grow beyond the canvas and become something a body might move through, rather than simply stand in front of?

An artistic director at the Norwich Theatre Royal said it best: “Space Hamlet was an amazing way of sharing the story of Hamlet to an audience that might otherwise not have been introduced to Shakespeare.”If you could ask Shakespeare a question about Hamlet, what would you choose to ask him?We'd ask him: "How do you feel about electric guitars, LED-lit space rocks and a golden robot playing your lead roles?" We like to think he was enough of a showman to appreciate the spectacle.What was the first piece of theatre that had a big impact on you?It probably was The Phantom Of The Opera. Somehow I had seen The Rocky Horror Picture Show way too young but that’s a movie, and it cemented a love for musicals but also for stories set in strange worlds to explore. Phantom has great music and design, but I think the storytelling is so focused it's like a laser that builds right up to that perfect final 15-minute scene. If our Hamlet aspires to anything, it's to have our score and our storytelling be something that builds up to the final duel scene where all the passions and energy at at explosive levels.What would you hope someone takes away from seeing Space Hamlet?We want audiences to leave energized, humming the songs and thoroughly entertained. Whether you know every line of Shakespeare or haven't read a word of it, we hope you walk away having experienced a fun, unique night of glam rock musical theatre while appreciating Shakespeare’s most intriguing work.Space Hamlet runs at The Cockpit Theatre in London from 22nd until 31st October 2026. For tickets visit https://www.thecockpit.org.uk/show/space_hamletYou can find out more about the show by visiting https://www.spacehamletmusical.com/

locator.quote: AC: All the theaters are so unique. And it depends on what type of theater it is. When I say that, I mean, is it a grid theater that has a fixed grid above, or is it a fly house that has a fly rail where you could bring scenery in and out from above? Is it in the round? Is it alley? Most designers would say they design for the space. You’re designing for the play, of course, but you also design for the space. What I mean by that is the size of the theater. An Importance of Being Earnest on an 80 foot wide theater is going to look very different from an Importance of Being Earnest that’s in a 20 foot wide thrust theater. You also want to fit the space, the set wants to fit nicely in the space as well. And with all that being said, the goal for us is always to focus on the actors. So a lot of the time in these bigger theaters, our goal is to focus in, to really keep our eye where the action is, which is the actors in the play.

locator.quote: At the heart of AuraLuxMuse are two key modules: Lighting-Aligned Music Pretraining (LAMP), which performs contrastive learning between audio and lighting cues for alignment, and Preference-Adaptive Mixture of Experts (PAMoE), which conditions preference-aware cue retrieval and adaptation on designers’ intent through a gated ensemble of style-specific expert networks. To support training and evaluation, we introduce Musilux, the first dataset of paired musical audio and professional lighting cue sequences under diverse performance scenarios. We evaluate AuraLuxMuse across both virtual simulation environments and professional-grade laboratories. Experimental results, including objective and subjective evaluation, demonstrate that AuraLuxMuse retrieves and adapts stage-lighting cues that are visually cohesive, semantically meaningful, and artistically expressive, showing its potential for AI-assisted aesthetic stage design.
